# Designing Better Agreements

*Make the promise clear enough to carry out and check*

::: {.chapter-epigraph}
> “And Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.”
>
> — Thomas Hobbes, [*Leviathan*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3207/pg3207-images.html), 1651, Part II, ch. XVII
:::

The buyer and supplier agree on a promising package: a volume commitment, flexible call-offs, shared capacity investment, and a defined exception to exclusivity. Then the buyer asks for an urgent extra batch. The supplier says the forecast came too late; the buyer says flexibility was the point of the agreement.

Both may remember the deal accurately while assuming different operating rules. Before signing, they need to decide what counts as an accepted order, who confirms capacity, and what happens when a commitment is missed. This chapter starts with that practical task, adding complexity only when it solves a specific problem.

::: {.callout-note .core-idea icon=false}
## Core Idea

For each material promise, specify who is responsible, what will be observed, how it will be checked, and what happens when circumstances change or performance fails. These operating decisions make an agreement usable. Additional tools—alternative packages, contingent payments, protected disclosure, or third-party procedures—should answer a diagnosed need.
:::

## Learning goals

- Produce a minimum viable agreement covering ownership, measurement, verification, review, failure, and exit.
- Diagnose whether unclear priorities, forecast disagreement, sensitive claims, or process failure warrants an optional agreement-design module.
- Add an advanced term only when its measurement, incentives, authority, and implementation burden are defensible.

## Start with a minimum viable agreement

The chapter uses six required fields as its spine:

| Required field | Agreement-design purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Owner** | Assign the promise to a named role with authority and resources. |
| **Measure** | Define the observable event, metric, threshold, and deadline. |
| **Verification source** | Name the record, data source, inspection right, and challenge process. |
| **Review date** | State when the responsible parties will examine performance and who may approve a revision. |
| **Failure rule** | Define cure, escalation, consequence, and treatment of relevant external shocks. |
| **Exit** | Define termination rights, transition, surviving duties, and any appeal. |
: Six fields that turn a package into a minimum viable agreement {#tbl-agreement-six-questions}

For the supplier's forecast-and-capacity obligation, the minimum record could look like this:

| Field | Illustrative operating term |
| --- | --- |
| Owner | The buyer's demand-planning lead submits the rolling forecast; the supplier's account lead confirms available capacity. |
| Measure | Submission is time-stamped; capacity inside the agreed band is confirmed within two working days. |
| Verification source | Both parties can inspect the shared forecast, order, and confirmation log. |
| Review date | Operational leads review the record monthly; designated commercial sponsors approve any change to the band. |
| Failure rule | A buyer-caused late forecast moves the delivery clock; a supplier-controlled miss after confirmed capacity activates the stated cure and service-credit rule. |
| Exit | Repeated uncured failure activates the agreed termination and transition process, including treatment of dedicated tooling and surviving duties. |
: A minimum viable agreement for one supplier obligation {#tbl-agreement-minimum-example}

The record is deliberately small. It does not settle every legal question, and legal drafting still requires the relevant expertise and jurisdiction. It does make the operational promise testable before complexity accumulates.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Add an advanced module only for a diagnosed problem

| Diagnosed problem | Optional module | Use only if... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The parties do not know which issues the other side values most | Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs) | The packages are sincere, understandable, and approximately equivalent to the offer-maker |
| The parties make materially different forecasts | Contingent term | The outcome is measurable, verifiable, sufficiently controllable, and worth the contracting burden |
| Important information is sensitive or a claim is consequential | Staged disclosure and claim verification | Disclosure is reciprocal or protected and a credible verification path exists |
| Agenda, authority, communication, or impasse blocks progress | Process or third-party rule | Decision rights, confidentiality, timing, and transfer of control can be specified |
| A signed agreement may leave mutually beneficial trades unexplored | Protected post-settlement search | The signed agreement remains the fallback and either party may stop without penalty |
: Route a diagnosed agreement problem to an optional module {#tbl-agreement-module-routing}

If no diagnosed problem fits a module, do not add one. Complexity creates interpretation, monitoring, gaming, and enforcement costs of its own.
:::

## Optional module 1: Reveal priorities through packages

One powerful tool for discovering integrative agreements is the use of multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, or MESOs.

A MESO is a set of two or more offers made at the same time, each designed to be roughly equal in value to the offer-maker but different in how value is allocated across issues. The other side’s reaction can provide clues to its priorities.

The supplier might offer three packages it has privately valued as roughly equivalent:

- **Capacity package:** lower unit price, firm annual minimum, narrow monthly call-off band.
- **Flexibility package:** higher unit price, wider call-off band, quarterly forecast commitment.
- **Investment package:** middle unit price, buyer contribution to dedicated tooling, longer term, and an exit schedule for unrecovered investment.

The buyer can compare these trade-offs without disclosing its reservation value. Its choice gives the supplier a starting point for a more specific question.

A comparison can teach the supplier which trade the buyer prefers, while giving the buyer several workable ways to proceed. Research has found economic and relational benefits from MESOs in studied bargaining settings (Leonardelli et al., 2019), but a preference is still a clue to investigate. If several terms differ, the choice alone cannot identify which term drove it.

Prepare the packages carefully. Approximate equivalence is from the offer-maker’s perspective, not an assurance that the counterpart will regard them as equally attractive. Each must be sincere and understandable; a deliberately unavailable decoy would undermine the exchange.



### Turn a package into a diagnostic question

Return to the supplier’s capacity and flexibility packages. Ask which is closer to the buyer’s needs, then ask why. A preference for flexibility might reflect expected demand variation, reluctance to commit cash, or a hidden approval constraint.

A useful next question isolates one trade: “If we widened the call-off band, could you accept a longer forecast commitment?” The answer gives more information than simply treating the first package choice as a stable priority ranking.





## Optional module 2: Use contingent terms when forecasts differ {#use-contingent-terms-when-forecasts-differ}

![This author's prescriptive synthesis shows four agreement-design tools together with the conditions that make each defensible. The figure is a design checklist, not a validated universal sequence or a claim that the tools necessarily improve an agreement.](../figures/agreement-design.svg){#fig-agreement-design fig-alt="Four panels summarize conditions for package offers, contingent terms, protected post-settlement search, and governance. A footer asks the reader to test the whole package against alternatives, feasibility, fairness, consent, and implementation."}

The conditions in @fig-agreement-design are substantive. A MESO is informative only when its packages are sincere, understandable, and approximately equivalent to the offer-maker; a preference is a clue, not proof of a stable priority. A contingent term is useful only when the outcome can be measured and verified, incentives and control are aligned, enforcement is credible, and sabotage and risk-bearing remain acceptable. Post-settlement search protects rather than reopens the signed deal only when the parties explicitly and voluntarily preserve it as the fallback. None of these tools substitutes for comparing the package with each BATNA or testing feasibility, fairness, legality, consent, and implementation.

A **contingent contract** makes a term depend on a future outcome. Suppose a builder expects early completion while a buyer fears delay. A bonus for finishing early and compensation for specified delays may offer each something it values, provided the possible payments, risks, and incentives are acceptable. Confidence alone does not make the arrangement beneficial.

The main questions concern measurement and control. Define completion so that speed cannot be achieved by omitting quality checks. Specify which delays the builder controls, how external disruptions are treated, who verifies the date, and how a disputed finding can be challenged. A payment tied to a vague “successful launch” simply moves the disagreement into the future.

Contingent terms also create new incentives. A party that controls the measurement or part of the outcome may be able to influence the payment in ways the other did not intend. The contracting and verification burden must be worthwhile relative to a simpler fixed term (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).



### Apply the logic to supplier capacity

The buyer expects monthly demand to remain within a narrow band. The supplier expects volatile peaks that would require overtime and displaced orders. Arguing about whose forecast is right will not create capacity. A contingent term can allocate the consequence:

- The buyer supplies a rolling twelve-week forecast and commits only to the first four weeks.
- Volume inside the agreed band receives the base price.
- Volume above the band is accepted only when capacity is confirmed and carries a predeclared surge price.
- If the buyer's committed forecast arrives late, the delivery clock moves by the same number of days.
- If the supplier confirms capacity and then misses a dependency it controls, service credits apply; repeated failure activates cure and exit rights.

This term turns forecast disagreement into a measurable allocation of responsibility. It still needs definitions: what counts as a forecast, confirmation, surge volume, supplier-controlled delay, external shock, and cure? The agreement should avoid cliffs that reward strategic reporting just above or below a threshold. When parties disagree about the future, let future evidence affect terms only when measurement, control, incentives, and enforcement are credible (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).

## Optional module 3: Stage disclosure and verification {#stage-disclosure-and-verification}

Integrative negotiation needs information, but disclosure can create vulnerability. Stage it. Begin with interests and lower-risk priorities that explain a position—“Delivery reliability matters because our customer contract contains penalties”—and ask for comparable information. Use the answer to propose a trade, not to impose the maximum pressure it reveals. Exact reservation values and confidential alternatives remain private unless disclosure produces a clear process, legal, or agreement benefit.

Trust is updated through response. If a disclosed concern is immediately exploited, future disclosure stops. If it generates a reciprocal question, verification path, or useful package, additional openness becomes safer. The goal is neither confession nor blind trust. It is enough validated information to design terms that can be observed and governed.

### Ask before inferring

Chapter 33 distinguished perspective-taking from perspective-getting. Imagination can reduce egocentrism and improve strategic thinking, but it can also project one's own priorities onto the counterpart; direct questions provide new, correctable evidence (Eyal et al., 2018; Galinsky et al., 2008). Ask what a term protects, who must approve it, what risk worries the other side, and what implementation success would look like. Partial or strategic answers remain possible, so verify consequential claims and reward useful disclosure with reciprocity rather than immediate exploitation.

### Culture changes the meaning of a move

Culture, profession, organization, and law can change what a move means. Directness can signal efficiency or disrespect; silence can mean refusal, consultation, deference, or thought; a concession can invite reciprocity or threaten face. Cross-cultural negotiation studies support attention to such variation but do not license reading a group average as a counterpart's personality, and common measures do not predict joint gains uniformly across settings (Brett & Okumura, 1998; Brett et al., 2021).

Return to the **Meaning Audit** in [Culture and Identity](29-culture-and-identity-the-same-action-is-not-the-same-act.qmd). Treat cultural knowledge as a hypothesis and ask how this interaction works:

- How is disagreement expressed safely here?
- Who must be consulted before a proposal can become a commitment?
- Does “yes” mean agreement, acknowledgment, or willingness to continue?
- Which terms need explicit definition rather than assumed shared meaning?
- Would a public concession, correction, or apology impose an avoidable face cost?

The prescriptive rule is simple: use group-level evidence to generate questions, then test meaning, authority, and consent in the particular interaction (Gunia et al., 2016).

### Replace lie detection with claim verification

Negotiation creates incentives to manage information. A person may lie by commission, omit a material fact, answer a different question, or use literally true statements to create a false impression—the practice called *paltering* (Rogers et al., 2017). But privacy is not automatically deception. A negotiator may decline to reveal a reservation value, private preference, or confidential alternative without making a false claim.

The dangerous response is to become a human lie detector. A meta-analysis of 206 documents involving 24,483 judges found average unaided truth–lie classification of 54 percent: 47 percent of lies were identified as deceptive and 61 percent of truths as truthful (Bond & DePaulo, 2006). Reviews conclude that nonverbal cues to deception are faint and unreliable (Vrij et al., 2019). A pause, gaze shift, nervous movement, polished delivery, or confident tone does not reliably diagnose deceit. Such behavior can also reflect stress, memory search, language, status, culture, or fear of being disbelieved.

![Beliefs about behavioral “tells” can be much stronger than the observed associations. The observed points reproduce all nine behaviors in the source comparison; student and professional belief estimates were available for seven, but were not reported there for nodding or hand movements. The values describe group-level associations and beliefs—not the diagnostic accuracy of a cue for an individual person. No single behavior proves that someone is lying. Original redraw of Sporer and Schwandt (2007), Figure 1.](../figures/lie-cues-belief-gap.svg){#fig-lie-cues-belief-gap fig-alt="A dot plot reproduces nine observed meta-analytic correlations for nonverbal behaviors and, where the source reports them, belief effect sizes for students and professionals. Observed correlations range from minus point one nine to point zero six. Beliefs are often much larger, especially for adaptor, foot and leg, gaze-aversion, blinking, and illustrator cues. The source comparison reports no belief estimates for nodding or hand movements, which are explicitly marked as unavailable. A side panel says that association is not diagnosis and recommends verifying claims rather than reading demeanor." width="96%"}

This is the same inference problem developed in [The Predictive Mind](04-the-predictive-mind-perception-is-inference.qmd), [Beliefs That Defend Themselves](10-beliefs-that-defend-themselves.qmd), and [Communication Is Joint Inference](33-communication-language-is-not-a-file-transfer.qmd). Suspicion supplies a prior; ambiguous behavior then appears to confirm it. The correction is not greater confidence in reading people. It is a better evidence path.

For every material claim, ask:

1. What exactly has been asserted, and what has merely been implied?
2. What record, date, document, authority, reference, test, or independent source could verify it?
3. Can the claim become a representation, warranty, milestone, inspection right, or contingent term?
4. What happens if the claim is mistaken rather than deceptive?

Direct questions can reduce deception, but they do not guarantee truth. Schweitzer and Croson (1999) found an overall reduction in deception in their first study; in their second, direct questions particularly reduced omission but could increase lies of commission. Therefore ask a precise question **and** verify the answer when it matters. Good agreement design makes important claims testable without pretending that every inconsistency reveals intent.

## Optional module 4: Negotiate the process {#negotiate-the-process}

A promising package can fail because the wrong people are in the room or because tentative suggestions are treated as commitments. Agree early on who can approve terms, which information is confidential, and when a proposal becomes binding.

For the supplier discussion, the buyer might say: “Could we first list the issues and compare two complete packages? Our planning leads can test capacity, while the commercial sponsors approve any price or volume commitment.” This allows operational knowledge into the search without confusing expertise with authority.

Record how an impasse will be handled as well. A pause for data, an internal approval, or an outside facilitator solves a different problem from another price concession. Revisit earlier assumptions when new information changes the package’s value; a process diagram should not make agreement feel predetermined.



[]{#third-party-dispute-resolution}

::: {.callout-note .research-lens icon=false}
## Optional module: when direct negotiation needs a third party

A third party can repair a process or replace it. These are different interventions. The mediation–arbitration distinction below follows the non-adjudicatory versus adjudicatory allocation of authority used in the UNCITRAL frameworks; the fit and risk columns are the author's decision aid, not comparative-effect estimates (UNCITRAL, 2022).

| Process | Third party's primary role | Who controls the outcome? | Best fit | Central risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mediation** | Structure communication, clarify issues, test assumptions, and help the parties search for settlement | The parties: the mediator does not ordinarily impose a settlement | The parties still need a negotiated solution, especially when communication, trust, emotion, or option search has stalled | Power imbalance, strategic delay, pressure to settle, or no agreement |
| **Arbitration** | Hear the parties' submissions and decide the dispute under agreed rules | The arbitrator or tribunal, to the extent specified by the agreement, rules, and governing law | The parties need finality, authoritative interpretation, or a decision after bargaining has failed | Loss of outcome control, cost, adversarial escalation, and a result neither party would have designed |
: Author decision aid: mediation assists party choice; arbitration transfers decision authority {#tbl-34-third-party-processes}

Mediation is therefore not “soft arbitration,” and arbitration is not “strong mediation.” A mediator can reframe, carry proposals, surface interests, manage difficult interaction, and reality-test a package while leaving acceptance to the parties. An arbitrator receives authority to decide. The precise legal effects, confidentiality, review, and enforceability depend on the clause, institutional rules, governing law, and jurisdiction.

Evidence does not justify treating mediation as universally superior. A 2012 review of the preceding decade found diverse goals, settings, mediator strategies, and outcomes, but relatively few controlled studies comparing specific strategies or observing actual mediation behavior (Wall & Dunne, 2012). It remains a boundary on what that literature had established, not a current comparative-effect estimate. Choose the process by its task: **Do the parties need help making a joint decision, or do they need someone else to make a decision?**

A staged commercial clause might move from operational leads, to executive sponsors, to mediation, and finally to arbitration or litigation. It should specify the triggering dispute, decision authority, time limits, interim obligations, applicable rules, and how urgent action can be taken. Legal drafting requires advice for the relevant jurisdiction; the design principle is to make the transfer of control explicit.

Hybrid procedures such as mediation–arbitration offer a settlement opportunity plus finality and may produce perceived time or cost savings in some disputes. They also create a predictable problem when one person performs both roles: information disclosed to a mediator in confidence may appear relevant when that person later becomes the decision-maker. Parties may become less candid or doubt impartiality. Barsky (2013) analyzes these risks in family-law disputes; recent American Arbitration Association commercial-practice guidance identifies the same concerns about candor, ex parte information, informed consent, and the integrity of an eventual award (American Arbitration Association, 2025). If a hybrid is used, the parties should decide in advance whether separate neutrals will serve, what information can cross stages, and whether renewed consent is required before the role changes. Potential speed should not hide a change in authority or confidentiality.
:::

### Optional extension: search safely after agreement

A **post-settlement settlement** searches for a mutually preferred replacement after an initial agreement is secure. The essential condition is explicit: the existing agreement remains in force unless every required party voluntarily accepts the replacement, and either party can stop the search without penalty.

The buyer and supplier might discover that a different payment schedule releases cash or reduces risk for both. They can investigate that trade without surrendering the terms already secured. If one side uses the search to reopen settled concessions under pressure, the protection has failed.

Use the procedure only when the original agreement is secure, participants have authority, and the possible gain justifies further effort. It is an opportunity to improve the deal, not an obligation to keep negotiating after “yes.”



## Complete the minimum agreement: implementation and review

### Ethics of value creation

Mutual-gain language does not establish mutual benefit. Examine whether the package makes material costs visible, preserves meaningful refusal, and assigns responsibility to someone able to carry it. A contingent bonus may encourage effort or encourage gaming; a menu may reveal priorities or hide an unattractive common term.

Ask each side to explain the agreement and its failure rules in its own words. If the explanations differ, resolve the discrepancy before relying on the signature. Legal enforceability and disclosure duties require advice for the relevant jurisdiction; operational clarity supports that work but does not replace it.



### Turn the supplier package into operating rules

Return to the opening disagreement about the urgent batch. “Flexible call-offs” becomes usable when the agreement specifies the permitted volume band, forecast deadline, confirmation procedure, and surge price. A shared record then shows whether the buyer requested capacity, whether the supplier accepted it, and which clock started.

The following priority map can be used to question the proposed terms. Its entries are illustrative guesses to verify with the counterpart, rather than facts inferred from the labels “buyer” and “supplier.”



The package becomes implementable only after the parties name owners, evidence, and review. The buyer owns the rolling forecast; the supplier confirms capacity within two working days. A shared dashboard records committed volume, accepted surge orders, defects, and dependency delays. A monthly operating review handles forecasts and quality; a quarterly governance review can revise bands and investment milestones. Cure periods precede exit except for safety or fraud. Disputes escalate first to named operational leads, then commercial sponsors, then the agreed formal mechanism. The agreement records which terms survive termination and how dedicated-tooling value is recovered.

Agreement architecture therefore completes six fields: **owner, measure, verification source, review date, failure rule, and exit**. A deal is not complete when it looks clever on paper. It is complete when the parties can carry it out, detect failure, and adapt without inventing a new negotiation each time.

| Issue | My position | My interest | My priority | Their likely position | Their likely interest | Their likely priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Lower | Budget constraint | High | Higher | Margin/reputation | High |
| Delivery | Flexible | Planning certainty | Medium | Earlier | Capacity utilization | Low/Medium |
| Payment timing | Later | Cash flow | High | Earlier | Cash flow | Medium |
| Service level | High | Reliability | High | Standard | Cost control | Medium |
| Contract length | Flexible | Optionality | Low | Longer | Predictability | High |
: A multi-issue priority map {#tbl-34-1}

::: {.callout-caution .evidence-and-boundary-conditions icon=false}
## Evidence Boundary

MESOs can reveal preferences only when the packages are sincere, understandable, and close in value to the offer-maker. A preference between packages need not reveal a stable priority; strategic response, culture, and context also matter. Contingent terms work only when outcomes are measurable, verifiable, sufficiently controllable, enforceable, and worth the complexity. Cultural evidence describes distributions, not individuals. Demeanor does not reliably identify deception. Mediation does not guarantee settlement or fairness, and arbitration does not guarantee a correct decision. Signing does not establish informed consent, fairness, or implementation capacity.
:::

## Practice Lab

Produce a **one-page minimum viable agreement** for the supplier obligation most likely to fail. Complete its six fields: owner, measure, verification source, review date, failure rule, and exit. Then stress-test the record against one plausible failure and revise whichever field did not provide a clear response.

Choose **no more than one** optional module from @tbl-agreement-module-routing. State the diagnosed problem that justifies it and add only the information that module requires—for example, two or three sincere packages for unclear priorities, one measurable contingent term for forecast disagreement, or one explicit escalation rule for process failure. If no module is justified, record “none.” Multiple packages, full contingent-contract drafting, independent audits, detailed mediation or arbitration clauses, and multi-shock testing belong in an advanced agreement-design file, not in the minimum exercise.

## Take it forward


Return to the term in your agreement most likely to become disputed. Can both sides tell what was promised, how fulfillment will be checked, and what happens if circumstances change? Add the provisions needed to answer those questions, then check that the extra complexity has not made the agreement harder to carry out.
